title: Writing to a File
objective: Save data from your program into a file, choosing between overwriting and appending.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.chapterTitle: Files and Exceptions (file-handling and Storing Data sections)
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only; exception-handling is covered in Code Forge's Errors & Exceptions chapter. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Opening a file for writing needs a second argument to open(): the mode. 'w' opens the file for writing and starts it empty, even if it already had content — anything that was there before is gone.
'a' opens the file for appending instead, adding new content to the end while keeping what was already there. Reach for 'a' whenever you want to add to a file without erasing its history.
The write() method does not add a newline for you. If you're writing several lines, add \n yourself, or your text runs together on one line.

Code Forge runs Python in your browser through Pyodide, so open() writes into an in-memory virtual filesystem rather than your computer's real disk. That virtual filesystem starts fresh every run, so the examples below write a file and then read it back in that same run, just to prove what ended up inside it.
explanation.rule: Use mode 'w' to start a file fresh, and mode 'a' to add to what's already there.

examples.title: Writing a fresh file
examples.code:
with open('log.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Forge started.\n')

with open('log.txt') as f:
    print(f.read())
examples.note: Mode 'w' erases any existing content in log.txt before writing. The read-back at the end just confirms what was written — it isn't part of the writing itself.

examples.title: Appending to a file
examples.code:
with open('log.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Forge started.\n')

with open('log.txt', 'a') as f:
    f.write('Forge stopped.\n')

with open('log.txt') as f:
    print(f.read())
examples.note: The first block creates log.txt with one line, standing in for content that was already there from an earlier run. Mode 'a' then adds a second line without erasing the first — the final read-back shows both lines survived.

checks.question: What happens if you open an existing file in 'w' mode?
options: New text is added after the existing content.
The existing content is erased before the new text is written.

feedback.correct: Correct — 'w' mode empties the file first.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. 'w' stands for write-from-scratch, not append.

assignment.title: Shopping List
assignment.brief: Write write_shopping_list(items, path) that writes each item in the items list to the file at path, one item per line.
requirements: Open the file in write ('w') mode.
Write each item on its own line.
Do not print anything — the function only writes to the file.
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
write_shopping_list(['eggs', 'milk', 'bread'], 'list.txt')
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    with open('list.txt') as _cf_f:
        print(_cf_f.read(), end='')
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))
assignment.outputCheckLabel: list.txt contains each item on its own line after calling write_shopping_list

hints: Open the file with `open(path, 'w')` inside a with block.
Loop over items and call f.write(...) for each one.
write() doesn't add a newline automatically — add '\n' yourself.
